panels.title: 1 · Traffic & SLO
panels.description: Is the platform moving money at the expected rate, and is it inside the latency SLO?

panels.title: Admitted / rejected requests per second
panels.description: Admitted counts every request the edge let in (in-flight limiter and rate limiter). Rejected counts requests refused before any work, by reason. Under D47 the mix is 40% sale, 10% authorize, 10% capture, 15% status, 10% refund, 10% retry, 5% other.

panels.title: Rejected requests/s by reason
panels.description: Rejections split by reason: auth (401/403), not_found (404), invalid_state (409/422), rate_limit (429), busy (503). busy currently absorbs inflight_cap, pool_wait and lock_timeout. A rising rate_limit or busy means the platform is shedding load.

panels.title: Completed payments/s by outcome
panels.description: Payments that reached a final, committed answer, by outcome. Per D47 a capture does not count as a second completed payment; 'captured' also includes one-call sales. 'declined' is a committed answer from the PSP, not a platform fault.

panels.title: Requests inside the 100 ms SLO
panels.description: Share of requests whose platform overhead is at or under the 100 ms p99 target, over the last 5 minutes. The SLO in docs/architecture.md is p99 <= 100 ms and p50 <= 25 ms, excluding PSP time. Below 99% the SLO is being missed.

panels.title: 2 · Latency
panels.description: Where the time goes: the platform's own overhead versus the PSP's. The SLO applies to platform overhead only.

panels.title: Platform overhead p50/p95/p99
panels.description: Total request time minus PSP wait, so these are the milliseconds the platform owns. Dashed lines are the targets from docs/architecture.md: p50 <= 25 ms, p99 <= 100 ms. A healthy p50 with a p99 above 100 ms is a tail problem, not a capacity problem.

panels.title: PSP wait p50/p95/p99
panels.description: Time spent inside the PSP adapter call. The PSP is outside the SLO, but a rising p99 here explains a rising end-to-end time and points at the dependency, not the platform. The local mock answers in a fixed 200 ms.

panels.title: In-flight requests
panels.description: Requests currently inside the edge. The cap is INFLIGHT_CAP (500 by default); once it is reached the limiter admits nothing and rejections with reason busy take over. A flat line at the cap means the platform is saturated, not slow.

panels.title: 3 · Saturation & runtime
panels.description: Is the API running out of threads, CPU, memory or allocation headroom before it shows up as latency?

panels.title: ThreadPool queue depth
panels.description: Pending ThreadPool work items. A queue that stays above zero is the earliest sign that requests are waiting for a thread rather than for the database. Small transient spikes under load are normal.

panels.title: Gen 2 GC per second
panels.description: Gen 2 collections per second since process start. Gen 2 is a full blocking collection: any steady rate under payment load correlates with the p99 spikes in the latency row. Zero is the healthy steady state.

panels.title: Managed allocation rate
panels.description: Bytes allocated per second since process start. High allocation is what eventually forces Gen 2 collections; this is the leading indicator for the panel on its left.

panels.title: API CPU
panels.description: Process CPU time per second, in cores. One core is one fully busy core. Compare against the CPU budget for the cell rather than against a fixed number.

panels.title: API resident memory
panels.description: Resident working set. Memory should be flat between deployments and grow only with caches or fragmentation. A sawtooth that never returns to baseline is a leak; a step change is a deployment.

panels.title: OS threads
panels.description: Operating-system threads in the API process. A jump with no change in load means thread-pool starvation or blocked I/O, and usually shows up in the ThreadPool queue first.

panels.title: 4 · Database & durability
panels.description: Is PostgreSQL healthy, and are committed payments durable? Zero deadlocks alone does not prove either.

panels.title: Database transactions/s
panels.description: Commit and rollback rate on the payments database. Under D47 each payment is several transactions, so this is several times the payment rate. A rollback rate that drifts up means conditional updates or constraint checks are fighting.

panels.title: Database WAL rate
panels.description: WAL bytes written per second. Every committed payment is durable only once its WAL record is on disk, so this is the volume that fsync has to keep up with. A step change with flat traffic means more writes per payment.

panels.title: Database locks held
panels.description: Locks held on the payments database, summed across lock modes and relations. It is a pressure signal, not a correctness signal: a steadily climbing count with flat traffic points at longer transactions or missing indexes.

panels.title: Deadlocks/s
panels.description: Deadlocks actually raised by PostgreSQL, independent of the application's retry counter. Must stay at zero: docs/decisions.md sets deadlock_timeout to 100 ms so deadlocks surface instead of hiding as lock timeouts.

panels.title: Abandoned commits
panels.description: Commits still running after the commit wait limit (E1). Any value above zero is a paging condition: the outcome of that payment is unknown and a retry can double-capture. This mirrors the CommitWarning alert in deploy/compose/prometheus/alerts.yml.

panels.title: Commit warnings (5m)
panels.description: Commits that returned a replication warning in the last 5 minutes. A warning means the commit reached the primary but the standby acknowledgement did not come back, so the outcome is unknown. Mirrors the CommitWarning alert.

panels.title: PgBouncer waiting clients
panels.description: Clients queued for a server connection, by pool. Non-zero means the connection pool is the bottleneck and the API is waiting before it even reaches PostgreSQL. D1 sizes the pool; a sustained queue means the sizing is wrong or the pool is leaking connections.

panels.title: PgBouncer oldest client wait
panels.description: Age of the longest-waiting client in each pool. Waiting clients with an old max wait is a saturated pool; waiting clients that clear in milliseconds is normal contention.

panels.title: Unresolved operations by kind
panels.description: Payments, attempts and refunds whose outcome is not established (PSP_PENDING or UNKNOWN). Stage 1 has no reconciler, so anything here waits for a person: docs/runbooks/unknown-outcomes.md. No series means nothing is unresolved.

panels.title: Age of the oldest unresolved operation
panels.description: How long the oldest unresolved payment, attempt or refund has been stuck, by kind. CK5 tolerance is 60 s; past that it is an incident, not a delay. Mirrors the UnresolvedOperationAging alert.

panels.title: Unresolved money held
panels.description: Minor units held by unresolved payments, attempts and refunds. This is the number to read before deciding whether an unresolved backlog is an inconvenience or a financial exposure.

panels.title: 5 · Payment pipeline
panels.description: Is the state machine progressing, and are the emitters this row depends on actually running?

panels.title: Payments by state
panels.description: Current payment count by state. Not emitted yet: the metric is in docs/metrics.md but the reconciler that publishes it is Stage 2. An empty panel here is a missing emitter, not a healthy system.

panels.title: Outbox oldest age
panels.description: Age of the oldest unpublished outbox row, i.e. how long an event has been waiting to leave the database. Not emitted yet: the outbox publisher is Phase 3. Once it exists, anything over a few seconds is a stalled publisher.

panels.title: Transaction retries/s by SQLSTATE
panels.description: Retries by SQLSTATE: only 40001 (serialization failure) and 40P01 (deadlock) are retried, at most twice. A flat zero line means no retries are happening; a missing panel would have been indistinguishable from a broken counter, which is why the zero is explicit.

panels.title: Conditional updates that changed no row
panels.description: Conditional updates that matched nothing, so the caller re-read and answered from current state. This is the optimistic-concurrency conflict rate: a rising value with flat traffic means contention on hot payments.
